#3176. The Dynamo-Electric Principle: 160 Years of Powering Industry

How a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion helped shape the motors and generators that drive modern industry

Innomotics is a global leader in electric motors and large drive systems, operating from its headquarters in Nuremberg, Germany.

The dynamo-electric principle: one idea, 160 years, millions of motors.

This article is brought to you by Innomotics.

In the annals of industrial history, few innovations have demonstrated such remarkable staying power as the dynamo-electric principle. Discovered by Werner von Siemens in 1866, this groundbreaking principle remains fundamental to modern electrical engineering more than a century and a half later – and continues to shape the technology portfolio of Innomotics, a globally leading provider of electric motors and large drive systems. What began as a breakthrough in electromechanical energy conversion has evolved into a cornerstone of global industry – powering everything from brewery operations in Qingdao to high-voltage drive systems in petrochemical plants.

The year 1866 marked a decisive turning point, not only in the broader arc of industrial transformation but specifically in the realm of electric motion. At a time when Europe was entering a new phase of industrial transformation, Werner von Siemens pioneered the dynamo-electric principle – a breakthrough that enabled electric machines to generate their own magnetic field through self-excitation. This innovation transformed electric machines from laboratory curiosities into practical power sources, enabling the widespread electrification of industry and infrastructure that defined the late 19th century.

This electric motor from Innomotics was installed in the early 1900s at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China and supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions.Innomotics

The principle itself is elegantly simple: an iron core generates a stable magnetic field; a rotating coil is placed within this field; movement in the magnetic field induces an electric current; part of this current strengthens the magnetic field; and electrical energy is continuously converted into motion. This self-reinforcing cycle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

More than 160 years later, the same fundamental idea continues to power industrial applications around the world. Millions of motors operate reliably under demanding conditions, keeping production running across generations. The dynamo-electric principle made it possible for electric machines to convert electrical energy into motion (and motion back into electrical energy), creating the technological foundation for modern electric motors and drive systems.

Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) enhances stability and reliability by actively reducing vibrations.Innomotics

Perhaps no example illustrates this longevity better than the electric motor from Innomotics at the historic Tsingtao Brewery in China. Installed in the early 1900s during the early electrification of industrial brewing, this motor supported production processes for more than 90 years, operating continuously under industrial conditions. It became a powerful example of long-term reliability in real-world applications – a testament to how engineering ensures reliable motion across decades.

Continuity, however, does not mean stagnation. Sixteen decades after the original breakthrough, innovations continue to emerge that build upon this proven foundation. Two recent developments – the Active Vibration Control System (AVCS) and oil-lubricated rolling bearings (OLRB) – carry this spirit of innovation and ingenuity forward, a commitment that has been recognized with the German Innovation Award.

Innomotics’ patented Oil-Lubricated Rolling Bearing (OLRB) technology enhances reliability and reduces maintenance requirements.Innomotics

AVCS helps optimize high-voltage motor performance by actively decoupling motors from their foundations to reduce vibration issues. OLRB helps prevent rolling bearing failures from the start with continuous lubrication, supporting higher availability, less downtime, and long-term cost savings. These innovations demonstrate how the basic principle of 1866 can be enhanced through modern engineering to meet contemporary demands for reliability and efficiency.

For three decades, with over 25,000 units driving performance globally, Innomotics’ Perfect Harmony GH180 medium-voltage drive platform has supported reliable operation across industries. Its modular architecture enables efficient power control, high availability, and long-term performance. With thousands of installations worldwide, Perfect Harmony GH180 continues to build on a proven technological foundation, minimizing downtime and ensuring stable production.

Keeping critical motors running requires the right expertise and innovation spirit throughout the entire lifecycle. With Innomotics Customer Services, operators and plant managers gain the insights they need to maintain reliability and optimize maintenance strategies. Winding Lifetime Analysis (WLA) combines operating history, machine measurements, and physics-based modeling to assess the condition of the winding insulation and estimate its remaining useful lifetime. This enables informed maintenance decisions, reduces uncertainty, and helps minimize the risk of unplanned downtime.

The Perfect Harmony GH180 delivers efficient, reliable and flexible medium-voltage drive performance.Innomotics

What began as a breakthrough in 1866 still brings its value to modern industry. The dynamo-electric principle made efficient and reliable electric motion possible – and it remains the foundation of modern motors today.

As industries worldwide grapple with challenges ranging from energy efficiency to operational resilience, this 160-year-old principle continues to prove its relevance.

For plant managers and engineers seeking long-term performance in demanding applications, the message is clear: the foundation laid in the 19th century remains as solid as ever. What has changed are the tools and services built upon it – from vibration control systems to predictive analytics – all designed to extract maximum value from a principle that has, quite literally, powered the modern world for a century and a half.

Innomotics, carrying forward a legacy that spans the full arc of this history, continues to move industry forward with innovations that create real progress. The dynamo-electric principle may be 160 years old, but as the company’s portfolio demonstrates, it is far from obsolete. It is, in every sense of the word, still running.

Innomotics is a global leader in electric motors and large drive systems, operating from its headquarters in Nuremberg, Germany.

#3174. Cornelis launches CN6000 800G networking to rival Nvidia InfiniBand

Its new 800G network cards aim to stop costly AI chips from sitting idle while they wait for data.

Cornelis’s CN6000 network card and switch, which partner systems will use from early 2027.

Cornelis, which Intel spun out in 2020, has launched CN6000, a family of 800G network cards and switches for AI and supercomputers. It claims lower latency than Nvidia’s InfiniBand, based on its own tests. Partner systems arrive in early 2027.

Cornelis, a networking company spun out of Intel, has launched CN6000, a family of 800G network cards and switches for AI clusters and supercomputers, it announced this week. It is pitching them as a rival to Nvidia’s InfiniBand.

In large AI systems, thousands of chips must constantly swap data. If the network is slow, expensive chips sit idle. “Every minute an accelerator waits on the network is capacity our customers paid for and didn’t use,” said CEO Lisa Spelman.

The main card uses Omni-Path, a networking technology Intel dropped in 2019 before spinning the business off as Cornelis in 2020. Cornelis says the card can handle 1.6 billion messages a second. It also says it is 21% faster than Nvidia’s InfiniBand at passing a small message, though that comes from its own tests.

A faster single message does not mean jobs finish 21% sooner, since that depends on the workload. Cornelis also launched a card for standard Ethernet networks, which most AI data centres use, with support for the newer Ultra Ethernet standard due later.

The cards work with chips from AMD, Intel, Nvidia and Qualcomm. Dell, Lenovo and Supermicro are among the server makers planning to support them, with systems due in early 2027.

Networking has become a hot spot in AI. Nvidia has spent billions on optical links, Huawei is betting on wiring over chips, and startups such as Upscale AI are building ways to connect rival chips. AMD, a Cornelis partner, is also building rack-scale systems to compete with Nvidia.

At least three division leads could change hands in NFL Week 10, with the red-hot Steelers and Bengals set to face off for AFC North supremacy, and the Panthers and Saints set to reveal the best of a historically bad bunch atop the NFC South.

The clash between the Vikings and Packers could also end up reshuffling the NFC North pack, which is by far the strongest division in the league this season.

There's the small matter of Kirk Cousins' Minnesota return too, which in turn has belatedly pushed No.1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza to the Raiders fore.

Here's our pick of the top five NFL Week 10 games — and where to watch NFL online and on TV.

The only way either of these teams is making the playoffs is by winning the NFC South, which is on course to go down as one of the worst divisions in NFL history. Despite being two games below .500, the Panthers are on top. But their position is precarious. Lose to the Saints and they'll be at least four spots out of the playoff picture. Although Carolina have lost three straight going into Week 10, Bryce Young and Chuba Hubbard impressed in defeat last weekend. New Orleans defensive end Carl Granderson, however, was on fire in their narrow victory over the Browns.

If Kirk Cousins hits the ground running, this could be the game of Week 10. Two and a half years after his departure, he's returned to the Vikings, with whom he spent six years. He may be 38, but his 20 passing touchdowns rank second in the league, and his partnership with Justin Jefferson remains the most prolific in NFL history. He might just be the final piece of the puzzle. The Packers' running game may be hopeless, but with Matthew Golden and Christian Watson downfield, Jordan Love has been unstoppable through the air, and the Green Bay defense has exceeded all expectations without Micah Parsons. It's remarkable that they're third and fourth in the NFC North.

It's Fernando Mendoza time. It had looked as if the No.1 overall pick wasn't going to get a look-in this season, but all of a sudden Kirk Cousins has been traded away and the 23-year-old, who led the Indiana Hoosiers to their first ever national title and picked up the Heisman Trophy in the process, is the Raiders' undisputed starting quarterback. Although Cousins softened his entry by throwing three interceptions in his swansong, this ferocious Seahawks defense is one of the last units he'd have wanted to face in his first ever start.

The Cowboys' season is on the line in Week 10, and it just so happens that their rivals, the NFC-leading 49ers, could be the ones to put them to bed. But it's also a potential banana skin for San Fran. Kyle Shanahan may see this as a golden opportunity to bed in new acquisitions DeForest Buckner and Keenan Allen before the 49ers' schedule takes a rough turn, which means they might not be at their all-conquering best. Whether the Cowboys actually capitalize on any teething problems is a different question.

Both the Steelers and the Bengals are solidly in the playoff picture, but Cincinnati's footing will get that bit firmer if they're able to get the better of Pittsburgh in Week 10 and leapfrog them into the AFC North lead. They're both on fire right now, having each won four on the bounce behind the Steelers' elite defense and the Bengals' electric passing game. Pittsburgh's key strength, however, has been stopping the run, and less than a quarter of Cincy's yardage has been gained on the ground. Instead, Joe Burrow has been lighting it up through the air with Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins. But Mike McCarthy's men do have one major advantage, They're coming off a bye, whereas the Bengals have just got back from Spain.

Ice storms cause long outages because several exposures act together. Ice adds weight to conductors, hardware and structures. Wind pushes on the larger iced surface. Trees and limbs bend into the line and add impact and uneven load. Conductors may also gallop and lose clearance. This paper explains how these loads combine and why the complete line must be assessed, not a single component. It reviews a monitored winter test of three conductor systems. It also summarizes utility records from a major regional ice storm. Finally, it outlines how to choose corridors, plan restoration and keep crews and the public safe around covered conductors.

#3170. Alexander Rinke says Europe needs AI champions to share in the next wave of AI value

Alexander Rinke told the TNW Podcast that companies and public agencies want to own their AI weights. The Celonis co-founder and co-CEO also set out his test for real product-market fit.

TNW’s Cristian Dina (left) and Celonis co-CEO Alexander Rinke at HumanX in Amsterdam, 23 September 2026

Thirty years ago, Europe’s GDP was roughly on par with the US, Alexander Rinke told TNW. Today it is dramatically less. The Celonis co-founder and co-CEO does not want AI to make that gap wider.

Rinke spoke to Cristian Dina for the TNW Podcast at HumanX in Amsterdam on 23 September. Earlier that day he had joined a panel on stage called “Can Europe Actually Build Sovereign AI?”. Earlier guests include Steve Lucas of Boomi, Arvind Jain of Glean, and Daniel Dines of UiPath. The full conversation is in the video below.

Countries and groups of countries such as Europe want control over parts of the AI stack, Rinke said. They want to know where their data and their IP go. Europe also needs its own companies to take part in an AI economy that will be huge.

“We need to really foster local champions, not because we don’t trust the Americans or we think AI is going to kill us all. Just because we want to make sure we take part of the upside.” Alexander Rinke, Celonis

Celonis is one example, he said. Its headquarters are in New York and Munich, and it has more than 20 offices around the world, with a strong presence in Germany, Spain and the UK. Europe is “not a satellite for us,” he said.

For a company or a public agency, sovereign AI means owning its own AI, Rinke said. In the end, that means owning the model weights.

“They don’t want to give all of their data to any model to train on that data.” Alexander Rinke, Celonis

Every organisation is like a snowflake, he said, so its processes and their context are unique. That needs open platforms that can be installed in sovereign environments. Celonis keeps a customer’s process data with the customer and does not send it anywhere. It also helps customers tune open-source models for specific business tasks. For those tasks, he said, they can get the same or better results than with frontier models.

Rinke started Celonis 15 years ago with his co-founders, Martin Klenk and Bastian Nominacher. They first wanted to build models that could simulate how a business works. To feed a simulation, they needed to know how the business ran today, and companies could not tell them.

“So we built an x-ray machine that looks at the data the business generates and x-rays how the processes work.” Alexander Rinke, Celonis

Celonis now calls this process intelligence. It maps how work really gets done, across systems and outside them, so companies can redesign it with AI. The company has about 3,500 people, he said.

Celonis recently bought Ikigai Labs, an MIT spin-off. Ikigai builds specialised models for tabular and time-series data and for what-if simulation. A large language model can use them as a tool, Rinke said, for jobs such as forecasting a supply chain or deciding whether to settle an insurance claim.

Asked about an IPO or new funding, Rinke spoke about the next phase of growth instead. He pointed to the Context Model that Celonis launched and to the Ikigai deal. Celonis describes the Context Model as a living model of a business in motion, built from its operational data and connected to its strategy.

Many startup pitches claim product-market fit that the company does not have, Rinke said. His test has four questions. Is the product valuable? Is it uniquely valuable, or easy to replace? Is it repeatable, or custom each time? Will customers keep paying for it?

“It’s easy to say that you have. It’s very easy to put on a slide for VCs.” Alexander Rinke, Celonis

If the answer to all four is yes, the next step is what he calls product-market-people fit: the organisation needed to scale it. Scaling too early can grow revenue that does not last, he said, especially in a boom market like AI.

Celonis was his first real venture. The founders started it during their studies, and Rinke put his master’s on hold and never finished it. They bootstrapped for five years, and winning the first enterprise clients without references was very hard, he said.

Venture capital is a good idea if a company wants to move quickly, Rinke said. But it does not replace the work a bootstrapped company has to do.

“You shouldn’t build the company to raise capital. You should build the company for customers.” Alexander Rinke, Celonis

He now works much more closely with Celonis engineers than he did a few years ago. He oversees some technical projects himself and is involved in how the company adopts AI internally. Asked whether he is technical, he said: “Yeah, pretty technical.”

The new HomeView smart display gives you a way to interact with Siri AI, your HomeKit accessories, and more in a 7-inch square display form factor. It’s available in two versions. There’s one with a built-in base, and another that’s designed to be mounted on your wall.

When buying from Apple for delivery, HomeView in all four colors is backordered to the first week of December. Most Apple Stores, however, seem to have same-day pickup availability today, especially in silver and starlight. It costs $299.

On Amazon, HomeView is available for immediate delivery in Space Gray, Starlight, and Rose Pink. The silver model is backordered until later this month (and on the verge of selling out completely).

Meanwhile, the new Apple TV 4K is also available starting today. It’s powered by the A19 chip, up from the previous model’s A15 Bionic. It also has built-in far-field microphones, so you can now interact with Siri without using the remote.

The new Apple TV also supports Siri AI, enabling things like world knowledge and personal context requests. It’s worth noting that Siri AI is also coming to the second- and third-generation Apple TV 4K models via a software update.

The other flagship feature of the new Apple TV 4K is support for a four-HomePod surround sound system. You need four HomePod (2nd generation) or HomePod mini 2 speakers, arranged in matching pairs at the front and rear of the room.

Read my full review of the new Apple TV 4K for everything you need to know. The big takeaway, though, is that it costs $299, which may be hard for many shoppers to justify.

When buying from Apple’s Online Store for delivery, the new Apple TV 4K is backordered to the first week of December. Most Apple Stores appear to have some availability for walk-in purchases starting today.

Apple’s MacBook Neo sent shockwaves through the computing world when it launched at an initial price of $599. As a result, competitors quickly responded with similar budget-friendly yet premium-looking laptops. Two of the main ones I’ve reviewed are the Dell XPS 13 (2026) and HP OmniBook 5, the subjects of this post.

Like Apple’s humble laptop, these notebooks have sturdy and colorful aluminum casings instead of the monotone, cheap plastic shells usually associated with budget laptops. These Windows machines also deliver strong performance for everyday tasks like web browsing and video streaming, plus bright displays and long battery life.

If you’re a Windows user looking for a MacBook Neo alternative, you can’t go wrong with either the Dell XPS 13 or HP OmniBook 5, as they're among the best budget laptops. But which one is truly right for you? Below, I’ll detail everything you need to know about these laptops to help you decide which one to get.

The HP OmniBook 5 14 impresses thanks to its lovely design, sharp OLED panel, strong performance, and astonishing battery life. Though it lacks HDR and has a so-so webcam, it’s a worthy alternative to the MacBook Neo for Windows users.

The Dell XPS 13 (2026) is a budget laptop with few compromises, thanks to its sturdy, lightweight aluminum design, sharp, vivid touchscreen display, strong performance, and long-lasting battery life. Starting at $749, it's easily one of the best budget Windows laptops right now.

13.4-inch 2.5K (2560 x 1600) InfinityEdge touch display

1x HDMI, 2x USB-C, 1x 3.5mm headphone jack

The HP OmniBook 5 and Dell XPS 13 are both relatively affordable laptops, especially as we’re still in the middle of the RAM crisis that has driven up electronics prices. That’s important to keep in mind, as one of these Windows laptops has increased in price since launch.

The Dell XPS 13 originally had a sticker price of $699. Unfortunately, the starting configuration with 8GB of RAM and 256GB of storage now costs $749. Conversely, the HP OmniBook 5 starts at $649 with the same RAM and storage. At time of writing, HP is selling this configuration for $599, or the original price of the MacBook Neo.

Even if you opt for the higher-specced OmniBook 5 with an Intel Core 5 320 chip, 8GB of RAM, 512GB of storage, and a touch display, it’ll cost $749. Basically, you’d pay the same price as the starting XPS 13, but get a laptop with better specs. Right now, the HP OmniBook 5 offers better overall value.

Like the MacBook Neo, the HP OmniBook 5 and Dell XPS 13 have ditched the cheap plastic designs of older budget laptops. Instead, both notebooks feature the sturdy aluminum chassis you’d see on more expensive machines. Their ultraportable designs also make them perfect for travel.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

At 11.69 x 7.90 x 0.50 inches and 2.2 pounds, the XPS 13 is the smallest and lightest of the laptops I’m discussing here. Like I said in my review, Dell didn’t skimp on the XPS 13’s design, as it has the premium look you’d expect from the XPS brand. It’s also the thinnest XPS laptop ever. It comes in the relatively subdued Sky and Storm colors.

The HP OmniBook 5 is the larger of the two Windows laptops, measuring 12.3 x 8.62 x 0.46 inches. Despite its larger size, it weighs only 2.5 pounds. You can get the OmniBook 5 in one of four colors: Peony Pink, Smoke Silver, Soft Honeydew, and Starlit Blue.

HP’s laptop has the edge with port selection. While both laptops have a pair of USB-C/USB3 ports, the OmniBook 5 also has an HDMI port and a 3.5mm headphone jack.

Both laptops have excellent keyboards, but the OmniBook 5 arguably has the better one, since its keyboard deck is larger and the keys have thicker keycaps and less shallow travel distance. The touchpads on both are comparable and accurately register gestures, though the OmniBook 5's is just a tad larger.

Both laptops are sleek and elegant, but the OmniBook 5 is arguably more eye-catching thanks to its bolder color options. It also has a 180-degree hinge that goes all the way back, plus more ports than the XPS 13.

Both laptops deliver sharp image quality and vivid colors. Those are the core similarities, even though these laptops use different display technologies. Not to mention different panel sizes.

The Dell XPS 13 packs a 13.4-inch 2.5K (2560 x 1600) InfinityEdge touch display, while the HP OmniBook 5 has a 14-inch (1920×1200) OLED panel. These differences make the panels a bit tricky to compare.

The XPS 13 has a smaller IPS display, but it has a higher resolution. On the other hand, the OmniBook 5 has a lower-resolution, larger OLED display. All XPS 13 configurations have touchscreens, whereas on HP's laptop you have to pay $50 more for that feature, since touch is only available on the higher-end Core 5 chip.

What do our display benchmarks show? As you can see in the table above, the Dell XPS 13 has the brighter screen for SDR and HDR content. HP’s laptop doesn’t support HDR. Of course, both are literally outshone by the MacBook Neo’s much brighter display.

Color reproduction numbers for the sRGB and DCI-P3 color gamuts are well above 100% on the HP OmniBook 5. That means colors are much more vivid on its display than on the XPS 13. That said, the latter’s numbers are closer to 100%, so colors are more naturalistic.

Both touchscreens are responsive and accurately capture gestures and taps. The laptops are pretty equal here, though the OmniBook 5's touchscreen might be easier to use since you can lay the display completely flat on your desk.

To be clear, the HP OmniBook 5 or Dell XPS 13 aren’t built for demanding tasks like editing 4K video or playing graphically intensive games. These Intel Wildcat Lake-powered machines are designed for everyday work like using Google Docs, browsing the web, and watching videos. Basically, if you’re a student or a remote worker with a lighter workload, the laptops are ideal.

I used both laptops for work, and each handled my typical workload: dozens of open Chrome tabs, light photo editing in GIMP, and the occasional YouTube video. I only experience noticeable slowdown when I have 15 or more Chrome tabs open. But that’s only when I’m really pushing things. For the basics, neither machine hindered me.

In the Geekbench 6 CPU test, both machines have comparable single-core scores, but the XPS 13 scores slightly higher in the multi-core portion. For video transcoding (HandBrake), the XPS 13 completes the task about a minute faster than the OmniBook 5. The XPS also scored better on the Blackmagic SSD test.

Aside from SSD speeds, the MacBook Neo performed better overall in our performance tests. But between the OmniBook 5 and XPS 13 specifically, Dell’s notebook has the performance edge. That said, neither these Windows laptops nor the MacBook Neo is designed for high-end gaming, as the graphics and gaming benchmarks above show.

While the Dell XPS 13 might outperform the HP OmniBook 5, the latter has a huge advantage in battery life.

In our battery life test, which involves continuous Wi-Fi web surfing with the display set to 150 nits of brightness, the OmniBook 5 ran for 19 hours and 52 minutes! While the XPS 13 lasted an impressive 14 hours and 57 minutes (for a Windows laptop), that’s still nearly 5 hours less. The MacBook Neo doesn’t come close to matching the HP’s endurance.

The HP OmniBook 5 and the Dell XPS 13 have both raised the bar for what you should expect from budget Windows laptops. They’re both great for basic work and entertainment, just like the MacBook Neo that inspired them. For most people, either will suffice.

As for which laptop is the better MacBook Neo rival, it depends on your needs. The HP OmniBook 5 comes in various colors, has a vivid OLED panel, packs more ports, and has exceptional battery life. It also currently starts at $599 (down from $649).

Conversely, the Dell XPS 13 offers better performance, a brighter display with more natural hues, and a smaller, lighter form factor. However, it has a higher asking price of $749 than the OmniBook 5.

Again, both the OmniBook 5 and Dell XPS 13 do their jobs well. But right now, HP’s notebook arguably has the edge thanks to its more striking color options, sharp OLED panel, and lower asking price. Because of that, it's the laptop I'd buy.

How to choose a healthy Christmas cactus: 3 quick checks before you buy

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Few holiday disappointments sting quite like bringing home a vibrant Christmas cactus (or the spiky-leaved Thanksgiving cactus often sold alongside it in November), only to watch every unopened bud drop onto the table three days later.

While it is tempting to reach for the brightest, most open display at the garden center, plants pushed into early bloom in warm greenhouses rarely survive the shock of a typical living room without shedding their flowers.

A fast inspection right at the display bench is all it takes to separate a thriving winter showstopper from a stressed plant about to fail. Before heading to the register, run through these three simple checks.

While a pot bursting with open flowers looks like the obvious winner on the display stand, it rarely delivers the longest show at home. Specimens forced into early bloom under warm nursery lights tend to fade fast once moved into cooler, drier rooms.

Instead, look for a plant loaded with tight, swollen buds showing just a blush of petal color at the tips, ideally with only one or two open flowers to confirm the shade.

As Jocelyn Ho, plant expert at Palmstreet, explained to my colleague Camilla, “Tight, small buds mean more bloom time ahead. A few open flowers are fine, but not too many so the plant has time to grow and shine.”

Make sure the buds feel securely anchored to the stem tips. Loose buds that detach at the slightest brush, or a ring of fallen buds sitting on the potting mix, are a clear warning sign of draft exposure or erratic watering.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The flattened, leaf-like segments give you an immediate snapshot of how well the plant has been cared for. Healthy specimens feature deep green, glossy segments that feel firm and plump to the touch. Dull, reddish, or limp foliage points to prolonged underwatering or light stress.

While you're examining the pads, lift a few trailing branches to check the undersides and joints for cottony mealybugs or scale insects before they hitch a ride home.

Also check the potting mix by gently pressing your finger into the surface: it should feel lightly, consistently damp. Because holiday cacti are tree-dwelling rainforest plants rather than arid desert dwellers, bone-dry soil causes rapid stress, while soggy mix triggers root rot.

The main stems at the center of the pot reveal whether the root system beneath the surface is actually intact. Look down into the base of the plant to confirm the stems are plump, upright, and sturdy.

Wrinkled, soft, or shriveled tissue near the soil line usually means the plant spent weeks sitting in cold, waterlogged peat that has already compromised the roots.

Walk away from any pot showing brown calluses, translucent soft spots, or main stems that wobble loosely when gently nudged. For the fullest display, choose a compact, bushy plant with plenty of branching segments rather than a spindly, stretched specimen that has been starved of light at the back of the shelf.

Having trouble with your own Christmas cactus? Whether your buds are dropping early, the leaves are turning limp, or you just can’t get it to bloom again, drop your biggest holiday cactus headaches in the comments below and I'll look into what's causing it.

#3164. Sierra releases Poppy 1.0 as Shopify and Meta’s Muse sign on

The standard tells AI agents what they can do at a company, and Meta's Muse now looks for it first.

More than 100 companies have now signed up as design partners for Sierra’s Personal Agent Protocol.

Sierra has released version 1.0 of Personal Agent Protocol, or Poppy, a standard for how personal AI agents deal with companies. Shopify has turned it on for every store, Meta’s Muse agent now looks for it on every site, and more than 100 companies have signed up.

Sierra has released version 1.0 of Personal Agent Protocol, or Poppy, its standard for how personal AI agents deal with companies, the startup announced on Thursday. Shopify has switched it on for every store on its platform.

Poppy lets a company tell a visiting AI agent who it is talking to and what it is allowed to do, such as check an order or book a flight. Customers sign in through standard logins and decide what their agent can access.

Meta’s Muse agent, which more than 10 million people have set up, now looks for Poppy first on every site it visits. Sierra, the AI customer service company led by former Salesforce co-CEO Bret Taylor, says 60 more companies have joined, taking the total to more than 100. They include Delta Air Lines, Intuit, Salesforce and Zoom.

Shopify stores need to do nothing. Poppy handles the moment an agent arrives and identifies itself, while Shopify’s existing shopping protocol handles carts and checkout. The agent must ask the shopper before taking certain actions.

A few companies are already live. Banking firm Mercury lets agents check balances and start payments, which still go through the account’s approval rules. Turkish Airlines lets them check fares and find business-class upgrades, which customers approve before paying.

The rules are not final. Sierra calls it version 1.0, but the specification is still labelled a draft and allows changes that could break existing setups.

Sierra and Meta first unveiled Poppy in October. It is one of several efforts to set rules for AI shoppers, as Visa and Mastercard build ID checks for agents. Amazon, meanwhile, wants shoppers to use its own agent rather than Muse.

#3162. Top Wall Street analysts are bullish on these 3 stocks for strong long-term growth potential

Global stock markets have been volatile as investors continue to assess geopolitical risks in the Middle East, fundamentals and valuations of companies in the artificial intelligence (AI) market and key economic data.

Top Wall Street analysts help investors look past near-term noise and pick attractive stocks with solid long-term growth potential.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Credo Technology (CRDO) provides high-speed connectivity solutions for AI data centers. Robust AI-led demand for the company's copper and optical interconnects has boosted revenue, driving a solid year-to-date rally.

In his latest research report, Bank of America analyst Vivek Arya raised his price targets on major semiconductor and semiconductor capital equipment stocks, with the price target for CRDO jumping to $340 from $252 with a reiterated a buy rating.

The 5-star analyst noted that Credo is seeing continued strength in the demand for its AECs (active electrical cables) from major and emerging hyperscalers. Moreover, the company has additional growth opportunities in optical DSPs (digital signal processors), ZF optics, ALCs (active LED cables), and PCIe retimers. These products are expected to begin ramping up production and profits in 2027-2028.

Following a meeting with the company at the 2026 BofA Global Tech Conference, along with recent channel checks, Arya raised his sales outlook for Credo by 2%-11% for fiscal 2027-2028 and his earnings per share (EPS) outlook by 5%-15%. The improved estimates reflect a strong AEC market outlook over the next five years and the company's "bulletproof reliability and incremental nature of its optical portfolio."

Arya based his new price target on a price-to-earnings multiple of 34x 2028 earnings, compared to the prior valuation of 33x 2027 earnings, saying it reflects contributions from new product adoption in coming years.

Arya ranks No. 84 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 62% of the time, delivering an average return of 31.5%. See Credo Technology Statistics on TipRanks.

Next on this week's list is Facebook- and Instagram parent Meta Platforms (META). Recently, Meta introduced consumer and business paid subscription plans for its Family of Apps and a new suite of Meta One (AI) subscription offerings.

Following the launch, Evercore ISI analyst Mark Mahaney reiterated a buy rating on META with a price target of $930. Mahaney views the rollout of the new subscription plans as a revenue diversification initiative, which could have a modest impact on revenue and eventually an even greater impact on operating income.

The 5-star analyst explained that he doesn't expect these new offerings to significantly affect near-term revenue growth due to their phased rollout and potentially low initial conversion rates. But he believes that even modest adoption within Meta's massive user base (over 3.6 billion daily users) could evolve into a significant high-margin revenue stream over the long term.

Mahaney highlighted that META is among Evercore ISI's top three, large-cap long-term picks, alongside Amazon and Spotify. His channel checks remain positive on Meta. Moreover, Mahaney noted that the Mark Zuckerberg-led company is successfully using AI to enhance user and advertiser satisfaction, reflected in engagement and return on ad spend (ROAS).

"What we now have with Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp Plus subscriptions is another attractive greenfield monetization opportunity for Meta – one that is not captured in Street estimates," concluded Mahaney, adding that his 2028 revenue estimate is 5% above Wall Street's consensus projection.

Mahaney ranks No. 987 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 53% of the time, delivering an average return of 9.8%. See Meta Platforms Financials on TipRanks.

Another social media platform in this week's list is Pinterest (PINS). Guggenheim analyst Michael Morris recently reiterated a buy rating on PINS with a price target of $24, citing "continued usage health and strengthening U.S. advertising business, each supported by ongoing AI-powered improvements."

The 5-star analyst highlighted that Pinterest has delivered double-digit global user growth for ten consecutive quarters, with his May data analysis indicating particular momentum in the second quarter of 2026. Morris said his Q2 2026 revenue growth estimate is at the high end of the company's guidance range.

Notably, Morris expects double-digit top-line growth in the United States and Canada to continue as large retailers adapt to new tariffs and the company's heightened focus on mid-market/small- and medium business advertisers expands its revenue base.

Morris believes that the adoption of Pinterest's Performance+ AI-powered advertising offering remains a major growth catalyst, currently accounting for 30% of lower-funnel revenue. The analyst sees scope for further penetration of this tool as advertisers using the product are increasing spending at nearly twice the rate of non-users.

Furthermore, Morris believes that the tvScientific acquisition expands Pinterest's reach into connected TV advertising, expanding the value of the platform's users offsite. He expects tvScientific to add about 2 points to PINS' quarterly revenue growth through the rest of the year, given the impact of business's seasonality and its U.S.-only footprint.

Morris ranks No. 857 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 54% of the time, delivering an average return of 12.9%. See Pinterest Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

#3161. Anthropic says its AI safety scores depend heavily on how they’re measured

Its new guide to safety testing reveals a 34-point gap in how one Claude model handled self-harm conversations.

Anthropic says the same model can score very differently on safety tests depending on how they are set up.

Anthropic has published advice on building AI safety tests. It shows Claude Fable 5.1 behaved appropriately in only 60% of self-harm test conversations via its API, against 94% in the Claude app after a fix, and warns that many headline safety scores hide wide uncertainty.

Anthropic has published advice on how to build reliable AI safety tests, and it includes some unflattering numbers about its own models. The guide, out on Thursday, says a claim that one model is “safer” is only as good as the test behind it.

Before it released Claude Fable 5.1, Anthropic found the model sometimes hinted that self-harm could help people cope. It did so even while urging users not to self-harm and pointing them to human support. Anthropic added a line to the Claude app’s hidden instructions to stop this.

With that fix, Claude behaved appropriately in 94% of the test conversations in the Claude app. Through Anthropic’s API, where developers use the model without that prompt, the figure was 60%.

That gap is the guide’s main warning: the same model can score very differently depending on how it is set up. Anthropic also says its simple one-question tests are now too easy, with every recent model scoring 94% to 98%. It relies more on longer conversations instead, where Cisco found guardrails can crack.

Even those can mislead. Claude Opus 5 and Opus 5.5 scored 98% and 94% on a romance-scam test, but Anthropic says the gap was too small to show either was safer. It advises teams to decide what to measure before testing, check AI graders against human experts, and always show how certain a result is.

The guide also says Anthropic has stopped many tests that give models internet access, after its models reached the open internet and breached three companies during cyber tests. Anthropic released Fable 5.2 this week.

#3160. Security Bite: Apple details Secure Exclaves, a glimpse at its ambient computing future

9to5Mac Security Bite is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Making Apple devices work-ready and enterprise-safe is all we do. Our unique integrated approach to management and security combines state-of-the-art Apple-specific security solutions for fully automated Hardening & Compliance, Next Generation EDR, AI-powered Zero Trust, and exclusive Privilege Management with the most powerful and modern Apple MDM on the market. The result is a totally automated Apple Unified Platform currently trusted by over 45,000 organizations to make millions of Apple devices work-ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

Apple published a new security research post this week detailing Secure Exclaves, a new architecture built to handle what the company calls “ambient sensing.” The latter isn’t anything new. “Hey, Siri” has been using a version of this always-on listening technology for years. The difference now (particularly on newer devices like Apple Watch Series 12 and HomeView) is new features need far more data from your surroundings, and Apple has changed where that data gets processed.

Today, on most Apple hardware, wake-word detections run locally on-device on a smaller, low-power chip. But once it thinks it heard you say “Hey, Siri,” the main operating system gets involved to confirm and wake up the smart assistant for use. There’s nothing necessarily wrong with this process. The split second of audio is all processed locally and not sent to Apple servers.

The problem lies in Apple’s newer features that ask for a lot more from users than a wake word.

Person recognition on HomeView identifies who’s in the room by face and voice, and Siri Recap and Live Rewind need to keep a running sense of what’s been happening around you. That adds up to a constant stream of sensitive camera and mic data, and it needs a more secure way of being processed than anything Apple had before.

Much like the existing Secure Enclaves architecture for authentication, instead of passing operations to the main OS, Secure Exclaves (notice the x) run their own tiny, separate operating system. Raw data goes in and a simple “that’s Arin” or “that’s the wake word” is outputted back to the OS, everything else is thrown away. According to Apple, that data “cannot be accessed by the main operating system, apps, or Apple.”

The changes don’t stop there. In recent SB column, I mentioned how on iPhone, the green dot that appears indicating that the camera or mic is live is all software connected, not like the hardwired LED that exists on the Mac. Now on iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone Duo, and MacBook Neo, the camera and mic indicators now live inside this new exclave, meaning even a compromised OS shouldn’t be able to hide them for malicious purposes.

It’s apparent Apple is building toward this new level of ambient computing across every type of device when you read technical reports like this. Future AI-first products, like the heavily rumored AirPods Pro with inferred cameras, will most certainly built on this new Secure Exclave architecture.

Six years in, the Xbox Series X still beats the PS5 and Nintendo's Switch 2 where it actually counts

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I can already hear the comment section sharpening its pitchforks, so let’s get this out of the way early: yes, I know buying an Xbox in 2026 feels like backing the underdog.

Shopping for a console right now usually comes down to two predictable habits. Most buyers are either chasing Nintendo’s Switch 2 or automatically reaching for a PlayStation 5, a reflex driven by years of internet noise and Microsoft’s own occasionally muddled messaging. Even I fell for the Switch 2’s sturdier Joy-Cons and nicer screen at launch, but soon it was collecting dust.

Once you strip away the badge loyalty and look strictly at how you live with a console day to day, the Xbox Series X makes a strong case as the smartest purchase in gaming. Six years into its run, it has matured into a no-nonsense machine that I’d still pick over the PS5 and Switch 2 for everyday convenience, library value, and big-screen performance.

If you want sprawling RPGs and big-budget releases to look and run their best, the Series X still hits the sweet spot. Yes, I know you can dock the Switch 2 to a TV and it outputs 4K via HDMI, so please save the "well, actually" comments. I just don't enjoy playing massive RPGs on it.

I love my Switch 2 for party games with friends, yet when I want to sink 80 hours into a dense open world, a hybrid console still feels like a compromise next to the Series X’s 4K horsepower and steady frame rates.

Under the hood, the Series X also packs slightly more raw graphical muscle than the standard PS5. In plain English, its graphics processor can crunch more visual data per second (12 teraflops versus the base PS5’s 10.28). While both consoles perform very similarly in most games, that extra power on paper can give the Series X a slight edge in resolution or frame-rate stability in demanding titles without forcing you to pay extra for a PS5 Pro.

Then there’s the elephant in the room, literally. The PS5 is one of the largest home consoles ever made, and personally, I still find it an eyesore. Between the flaring white fins, awkward horizontal stand, and departure from PlayStation's classic all-black, it’s kind of a a nightmare to blend in. The Series X, on the other hand, is a plain, matte-black tower that doesn’t demand to be the centerpiece

Even with subscription prices fluctuating, Microsoft’s ecosystem still stretches my gaming budget further than anything else. Xbox Game Pass Ultimate packs in hundreds of titles alongside day-one releases from Bethesda, Xbox’s own studios, and select Activision games, giving me massive value for what I pay.

My favorite perk, though, is Xbox Cloud Gaming. When I don't fancy clearing hard-drive space for a massive download, streaming games instantly is like sampling ice creams before deciding which one I’m actually sticking on the cone — I’ve even had friends who don't own an Xbox use it to test-drive games before buying them on the PlayStation Store.

Pair that with Xbox Play Anywhere, which gives you both the console and PC version of supported games under a single purchase, and it easily justifies the cost for me.

I have four generations of consoles hooked up in my games room, and nothing beats the quality of life features baked into the Series X.

Quick Resume alone makes going back to a PS5 or Switch 2 feel strangely dated. I’m replaying Red Dead Redemption 2 at the moment, and just holding down the guide button on my controller to wake the TV, clicking the tile, and being dropped straight back into the saddle in seconds completely changes how you game. You can keep three games suspended like this at once.

Add in free cloud saves (which Sony and Nintendo still lock behind paid memberships) and backward compatibility stretching across Series X/S, Xbox One, Xbox 360, and the original Xbox, and the value adds up fast. I can literally play a lifetime's worth of my back catalog on one console.

Buying an Xbox in 2026 doesn't mean sitting out the year’s biggest moments. With GTA 6 arriving on November 19, the Series X gives you day-one access at full current-gen fidelity, something the Switch 2 isn't getting at launch, and even lets Xbox One owners stream it via Cloud Gaming (provided you own the game) while PS4 players are left behind.

People love to dunk on Xbox’s missteps, and putting its games on rival boxes has blurred the old console-war lines. Yet six years in, the Series X runs quiet, its library is stacked, unlike the Switch 2, where you're still betting on future software, and it does what it says on the tin and does it well.

The PS5 may win the popularity contest, the Switch 2 might own party nights, yet, for my money, the Series X remains the best all-rounder console in 2026.

Agree, disagree, or happily sticking with a PC? Let me know in the comments.

#3158. OpenAI launches ChatGPT Wallet, enabling ‘dot’ agents to make purchases

OpenAI is launching ChatGPT Wallet, which it says is “setting a new bar for secure payments by agents.”

ChatGPT Wallet works with OpenAI’s “dots” agent feature and includes a partnership with American Express, MasterCard, and Visa. Here’s how it works.

OpenAI says ChatGPT Wallet is the “first wallet that lets agents pay without access to users’ actual card details and that requires a security check for every purchase, while also preserving existing card rewards and protections for eligible disputes.”

“We’re starting with limited availability to ChatGPT Pro users,” OpenAI explains, “so we can learn from real-world use and work with businesses, banks, and payment networks to improve compatibility and reliability.”

The feature won’t work with websites that block agents, however, which has increasingly become an issue online.

Before each purchase, the user reviews the items, total, and selected card, then approves it with a security check such as Face ID or a fingerprint scan. Each approval creates a clear record of the purchase the user authorized the agent to make.

After the user approves, the payment network provides a payment token—a substitute for the user’s actual card details—with a card number, security code, and expiration date. The payment is charged to their selected card without ChatGPT Wallet sharing their actual card details with the business or agent.

You can read more about ChatGPT Wallet and how it works here.

The company emphasizes that payments are secure, card info isn’t shared with your dot or merchants, and that you’re in control of purchases.

iOS 27.2 arrived last month with new features for Messages, Apple TV, and more, plus two improvements for CarPlay. Here’s what’s new for CarPlay users.

Apple Podcasts in iOS 27.2 adds two new sections to the Home tab: ‘New Episodes’ and ‘Continue Playing.’

Essentially, Apple has rethought how the core ‘Up Next’ queue of its Podcasts app works.

Like you would expect, ‘New Episodes’ contains only the latest episodes from your favorite shows. But after you’ve started an episode, you’ll find it in the ‘Continue Playing’ row just below.

This overhaul to podcast management makes it easier to find the latest episodes of your shows and also pick up where you previously left off. I’m a big fan of the change.

Siri AI introduces a variety of upgrades in iOS 27.2, including two that carry over to CarPlay as well.

It can take some adjustment to remember that Siri AI is available in the car just like on iPhone. But CarPlay is an especially useful platform for Apple’s more powerful assistant.

It’s arguable whether this qualifies as an “improvement,” but it is a change worth mentioning. iOS 27.2 includes a new app icon for Apple Music, plus some minor design tweaks in the app.

These changes are related to the broader rebrand of Apple Music that was recently unveiled.

I'm a big fan of the commuting bubble. What is it? Well, it's what I've lovingly called the place I go to when I commute on public transport. As soon as I put on my headphones or dig my earbuds out of my bag, I slip into my own little bubble to focus on work, read a book, or (more often than not) lock in on transport delays and timetables.

And some of my personal favorite earbuds — from CMF by Nothing, Sony and Bose — are on sale for Black Friday. This year, with prices across tech climbing higher and higher it's nice to see some deals on products I can truly recommend.

I use each pair of earbuds for a different instance, whether I need focus or awareness of what's going on around me. Hopefully, they'll be able to help you create a commute bubble of your very own come Monday morning.

The CMF Buds 2a are some of the finest budget earbuds you can buy, at just $29, and even cheaper for Black Friday. The sound quality is impressive and the customizable ANC makes them a winner for daily use. Minor drawbacks, like the plasticky feel and lack of in-ear detection, are typical at this price point, and the overall performance makes them an excellent yet affordable choice — for $19, you really can't go wrong.

My favorite kind of journey is one where I can block out the surrounding noise and focus. Whether it's finishing off some work or getting stuck into my latest book, decent ANC is essential.

With the early Black Friday sales, you don't need to break the bank because you can pick up the CMF by Nothing Buds 2a for just $19 on Amazon — that's less than grabbing lunch at my nearest restaurant!

These buds also have EQ customization in the app, so the sound quality can be altered to suit you. But yes, the best part is the ANC. It's shockingly good, and it blocked out all of the ambient sound around me.

The Bose Ultra Open Earbuds are stylish open-ear earbuds that don’t compromise on audio features. They're very comfortable to wear all day, whether I'm at my desk or in the gym.

When I'm in a situation where I don't know my exact route, or there are cancelations happening because of the weather (more often than not), I need to be totally aware of my surroundings. Open-earbuds are the answer.

For the past few months, I've been keeping the Bose Ultra Open Earbuds in my bag, and they come in handy more often than you'd think. Being able to listen to my music in excellent quality while also paying attention to chatter and announcements around me is incredibly useful.

Bose are at the higher end of the open-earbuds market, but the price point is worth it, especially during Black Friday sales for $40 off on Amazon.

The Sony WH-1000XM6 are the flagship noise-cancelling headphones everyone should have. The 40-hour battery life can take me through most of the week, and the lightweight design makes them comfortable to wear all day long.

This is the ultimate "please don't bother me" option — the Sony WH-1000XM6. These over-ear headphones are the perfect balance between blocking out your surroundings and staying aware.

The noise-cancelling on these cans is some of the best I've used, but you can also switch modes to have the ambient sound loud and clear in your ears. This means that when I'm on a flight, for example, I can tune out the cabin noise and welcome it back in just before landing so I don't miss any announcements.

Out of the three earbuds and headphones on sale, the Sonys are the ones I reach for the most in my collection as they come in handy more regularly, but one of the other options may suit you better.

#3155. Nvidia and Dyania bring AI chart review onto hospital servers

Dyania's Synapsis AI runs on the hospital's own Nvidia servers, so patient records never leave the building.

Dyania’s Synapsis AI links findings across years of a patient’s records, according to Nvidia.

Dyania Health’s Synapsis AI reviewed the records of more than 7,800 Cleveland Clinic heart-valve patients, running on the hospital’s own Nvidia servers. The data was used to build a model predicting when replacement valves fail. Doctors still make every decision.

An AI system has read up to 16 years of records for more than 7,800 Cleveland Clinic heart patients, Nvidia said on Friday. It ran entirely on the hospital’s own servers. The software, Synapsis AI, is made by New Jersey startup Dyania Health.

Much of a patient’s history sits in doctors’ notes and scan reports rather than tidy data fields. Synapsis reads those notes and answers clinical questions, linking each answer back to the record it came from. It runs on Nvidia hardware inside the hospital’s network, so records never leave the building, much like a UK NHS triage AI built with Nvidia.

For the study, it answered 88 questions about each patient who had an aortic valve replaced between 2005 and 2021. The resulting data was used to build a model that predicts the risk of a replacement valve failing three, five and ten years after surgery. Nvidia says the chart review would have taken clinicians years by hand.

Lars Svensson, head of Cleveland Clinic’s heart institute, called it “a promising step towards enhanced outcomes and more personalized care for patients.”

Doctors still review the AI’s evidence and make every decision. The study shows the tool can build a dataset and predict risk, not that it improves care, and Dyania says it still needs outside validation. Cleveland Clinic is also an investor in Dyania, it disclosed last year when it rolled the tool out for trial recruitment.

Big tech is pushing hard into hospital records. Google Cloud launched Gemini for healthcare this week, and Bunkerhill raised $55M for hospital AI agents. But proven gains for patients remain harder to find, and doctors have pushed back on bold claims.

Garmin’s top adventure watches have different strengths

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Fenix 9 Pro is Garmin's flagship watch and offers a more attractive design than the Enduro 4, along with extra features and more choice in the size and display you get.

The Garmin Enduro 4 is cheaper and lighter than the Fenix 9 Pro, and offers better battery life too.

Buying one of the best Garmin watches brings with it some guarantees with regard to the features you can expect, especially at the higher end of the brand’s line-up, where the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro and Garmin Enduro 4 both sit.

These watches offer stellar sports tracking and training analysis, along with the best navigation tools you’ll find on a smartwatch thanks to their offline routable maps. They are also equally accurate with GPS and heart rate, in my experience, and run the same software.

However, after testing the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro and Enduro 4 extensively, there are certainly some key differences between the two in other areas, most notably design and battery life.

If you want more details on either watch, check out my Garmin Fenix 9 Pro review or Garmin Enduro 4 review, but read on for a summary of the differences between them I noticed when testing them individually and at the same time.

The biggest difference between the two watches is price, since the Garmin Enduro 4 costs much less than the Fenix 9 Pro.

You’ll pay $899 for the Enduro 4 right now, while the cheapest Fenix 9 Pro model is $1,099, whether you choose the AMOLED version or the Fenix 9 Pro Solar with a memory-in-pixel (MIP) display like the Enduro.

The key thing that the Fenix 9 Pro offers with its design is choice. It comes in three sizes — 43mm, 47mm and 51mm — and you can pick between an AMOLED or MIP display, and even choose between colors for the bezel and sensor guard.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

In contrast, the Enduro 4 comes in one style and size. It’s a 51mm watch with a MIP display, and it only uses titanium for its bezel, with a mostly plastic case, whereas the Fenix 9 Pro has a full titanium case.

This gives the Fenix 9 Pro a more elegant look, but it also makes it considerably heavier than the Enduro 4. I tested a 51mm Fenix 9 Pro AMOLED, and both it and the Enduro 4 are large watches, but the Enduro 4 counters that a little by being so light.

When it comes to the display, picking between AMOLED and MIP will come down to personal preferences.

I find AMOLED brighter and clearer in almost all conditions, and just as good as MIP in bright sunlight these days, and I prefer using an AMOLED watch in general, but MIP uses less power and is less obvious on the wrist, and the Enduro 4’s display was still clear enough to see at all times.

Both watches have sapphire crystal screens and built-in flashlights, but you get an extra green mode on the Fenix 9 Pro’s flashlight.

You also get a diveproof watch with the Fenix 9 Pro, which can be used to depths of 40m. The Enduro 4 has a high waterproof rating of 10ATM and is fine for swimming, but isn’t a diving watch.

Another addition on the Fenix line is a mic and speaker, which can be used to take voice notes and give voice commands to the watch.

One advantage of the Enduro 4 is that it ships with Garmin's fabric ComfortFit band as standard, which I much prefer to the silicone band on the Fenix 9 Pro. You can buy the ComfortFit band separately, but it will cost $59.

The design differences speak to the approach behind the two watches. The Enduro 4 is built to be simpler and lighter, which helps it to be more affordable, but the Fenix 9 Pro is the all-singing, all-dancing option with a variety of models to pick between.

The two watches share very similar sports tracking and training analysis features, and both have proved to be similarly accurate throughout my testing.

There’s only one difference worth flagging in this area, which is that the Fenix 9 Pro is a diveproof watch and has Garmin’s scuba, apnea and snorkel sports modes.

One of the biggest features you get on the Fenix 9 Pro (InReach model) that isn’t available on the Enduro 4 is LTE and satellite connectivity.

This feature requires a subscription but allows you to stay in contact with the world when you’re off the grid or phone-free, through messaging and the ability to send SOS alerts.

Otherwise, both watches share the usual Garmin smart features. They can store music and link to streaming services, make NFC payments through Garmin Pay, and have access to the Connect IQ app store.

Along with being cheaper and lighter, the main advantage of the Enduro 4 is its incredible battery life.

Whatever Fenix 9 Pro you opt for, including the Solar MIP watch, the Enduro 4 will outlast it in both watch and GPS modes, partly because it has a bigger solar ring than the Fenix 9 Pro Solar.

I've compared the 51mm models of the Fenix 9 Pro to the Enduro 4 below. Note that to get the full solar battery life listed, you need to be out and about in sunny conditions for three hours a day on average.

In my use, the Enduro 4 lasted me 16 days on its first charge and is tracking for 17-18 on its second charge, whereas the 51mm Fenix 9 Pro AMOLED lasts me 10-11 days with the screen set to always-on.

This was during the British winter too, when I gave the Enduro 4 almost nothing in terms of a solar charging boost, so you can expect the gap to be wider in sunnier climates.

13.3mm (43mm),13.8mm (47mm), 15.8mm (51mm)

10 days (43 mm), 18 days (47mm), 31 days (51mm) (raise to wake)

18 hours (43mm), 32 hours (47mm), 56 hours (51mm)

The Garmin Fenix 9 Pro line-up offers more features and choice than the Enduro 4, and I prefer the all-titanium design of the Fenix and its brighter AMOLED display.

However, the Enduro 4’s relative simplicity will appeal to many people, as will its lower price, longer battery life, and lighter design.

If you’ve been eyeing the Fenix 9 Pro Solar in particular and don’t really need the connectivity features on the watch, then I think the Enduro 4 is a better value buy. Or even the Garmin Enduro 3, for that matter, since it has a similar design and feature set to the latest model.

#3152. Apple Maps in iOS 27 has hidden new feature I’ve been loving

iOS 27 gave Apple Maps a handful of new features, and my favorite is one that keeps offering fresh updates every week: Local Lists.

Apple Maps has long offered a ‘Guides’ feature where you can browse curated collections of places worth checking out. Sometimes they’re created by Apple’s editorial team, other times by celebrities or in conjunction with current events.

But in iOS 27, there’s a new feature—Local Lists—that’s sort of an extension of Guides, but it gets updated weekly with the latest trending places.

Here’s how Apple describes it, via Apple Newsroom:

I’ve always enjoyed browsing Guides in Maps to help find new places. But Local Lists are a great expansion of the idea, especially since they’re updated all the time. I’m always up for trying a new trending restaurant, and now Maps makes it easy to stay on top of what’s new.

Even if you’ve been using iOS 27 for months, there’s a good chance you’ve never seen Local Lists. That’s because they’re pretty hidden.

To find the feature, tap into the search field in Maps and scroll down to see a new ‘Trending Restaurants’ section. On my iPhone 18 Pro, by default this section gets hidden behind the keyboard, so you have to first scroll and dismiss the keyboard to see it.

Trending Restaurants are ranked from 1-20. The search screen shows only a handful, but you can tap to view the full list. For example, if you open the ‘Trending Restaurants in New York’ list, you’ll see 20 places worth checking out.

How does a restaurant make the list? Per the in-app explanation, the list contains “Restaurants climbing in popularity this week, based on what people view, share, and interact with on Apple Maps.”

Since these Trending Restaurants lists update weekly, Apple says you’ll want to save any places you plan to visit. There’s a convenient + button next to each listing.

It’s unclear exactly how many different parts of the US have localized lists in iOS 27. But if you poke around and find the full collection of Local Lists, there are 1,021 total—so you’ll probably have one in your area.

You can browse all available lists by opening a Trending Restaurants list then tapping where you see the Apple logo and ‘Local Lists’ near the text that says when it was last updated.

Have you used Local Lists in iOS 27’s Maps app yet? Let us know what you think via the comments.

#3151. FBI reportedly probes software update behind US flight ground stop

A failure at all 22 US air traffic control centres stopped flights leaving any US airport for over four hours.

he FBI is looking at whether a software update caused Friday’s outage that grounded flights across the US, Bloomberg reported. The bureau does not believe a cyberattack or crime was behind it, Bloomberg said, citing one person familiar with the matter.

The Federal Aviation Administration stopped all flights from taking off on Friday after a fault cut links at its control centres. The halt lasted more than four hours and hit all 22 centres, which guide planes between airports, Al Jazeera reported.

It was the first such halt since January 2023, when an FAA computer system failed. Thousands of flights were delayed or cancelled, and the knock-on effects are expected to last all weekend.

No official cause has been given. However, multiple sources told CBS News that an update to the private network connecting the air traffic control system made it restart and then crash.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed old kit. At a press event on Friday evening, he said ageing systems had been flooded with data and failed, Axios reported.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said officials were checking whether old and new kit had failed to work together. He said there was no sign of a cyberattack.

Mullin also said the outage was not linked to a separate global Microsoft outage on the same day, CBS News reported.

The FAA is replacing much of its air traffic tech. It began using an AI congestion tool around Washington in September, though no source has linked that system to Friday’s failure.

#3150. This tiny iOS 27 camera feature really makes a huge difference

When shooting both photos and videos on my iPhone, I make regular use of a few different third-party apps, mostly because I like to take manual control.

But a combination of the new Pro controls on the iPhone 18 Pro and a new feature introduced with iOS 27 means there are more times when I can stick to Apple’s stock Camera app. If you aren’t already using customizable controls, I highly recommend doing so …

Developers know that a big reason for using third-party camera apps is being able to use them in much the same way you would a standalone camera. A key part of this is having easy access to manual control over things like aperture (on the iPhone 18 Pro), shutter speed, white balance, and choosing between manual and auto focus. Those settings are right there on the main screen of almost all third-party apps.

With the iPhone 18 Pro, the same set of controls are also available in Apple’s stock camera app. By default, these are tucked inside a menu, requiring an initial tap to open it. As we noted back in September, however, iOS 27 brings customizable controls to the camera app.

Simply open the menu and tap the Edit button (top-left when holding the phone vertically) and you can add any of the controls to the main screen. This makes them available in a single tap.

Aperture, shutter speed, and white balance as these are the three main manual controls I use. Exposure compensation, because sometimes the only reason I want to take manual control is to increase or decrease the exposure, and that provides a faster way of doing so (quicker than the alternative drag up/down within the photo, in my experience). Finally, I have one-tap access to the histogram to help in setting exposure.

It’s a similar story in video mode. I again have aperture and white balance along with exposure compensation and the histogram. But here I add instant access to frame-rate and focus modes (as I’m more likely to switch focus mode when shooting video).

Of course, third-party apps still have an important role, but this one change has made a big difference to me when using the stock camera app for both photos and video.

Do you make use of this feature yourself? If so, please share the details in the comments.

The answer all depends on the temperature

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Fall is in full swing, and if your yard looks anything like mine, you’re probably busy clearing scattered leaves while tending to a tired lawn.

What makes it look so worn down are probably the sparse, empty spots across the yard — which leaves me asking: is it too late to plant grass seed in November?

Luckily, I called on some lawn experts to shed some light on this and offer their advice on achieving a lush, resilient lawn even in this colder season.

So before you get ready to sow, here is what you need to consider before grabbing your seed packet and getting started.

While November is typically not the right month to sow grass seed, this can also depend on your regional climate, local soil temperatures, and grass seed type.

For instance, with cool-season grasses (such as Kentucky bluegrass, perennial ryegrass, tall fescue), you should only overseed once the temperatures drop below 50 degrees Fahrenheit.

“It’s not necessarily too late — but it is more of a riskier time to do so,” advises Chris Bonnett, founder of GardeningExpress. “If you are planting grass seed this month, timing is everything, and it will depend on what the weather is like where you are.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

“The soil temperature is the most important thing, as the seeds will need a mild environment to germinate, and you'll need the soil temperatures to be consistently around 46.4 °F to 50 °F or above for germination.”

"If you are planting grass seed this month, timing is everything, and it will depend on what the weather is like"

On the other hand, warm-season varieties like Bermuda grass, zoysiagrass, centipedegrass, and Bahiagrass begin going dormant as the weather cools down. As a result, planting them during cold spells reduces their chances of growing. This is especially the case during colder snaps and the risk of frost.

"Seed should be planted at least 6 weeks before the area's first hard frost, so it has time to germinate and build some root growth before winter dormancy sets in," advises Matthew Koch, Ph.D., research and development at ScottsMiracle-Gro.

"Seed should be planted at least 6 weeks before the area's first hard frost

"Regions that experience a milder fall, also known as the Transition Zone (roughly Kansas through the Mid-Atlantic, including areas extending toward the Carolinas), might be able to have one final feeding before winter, but it is entirely dependent on the local climate, growing conditions, and grass type."

However, if the soil is too cold, experts suggest waiting until warmer weather begins during springtime. “I’d recommend waiting until the spring, adds Bonnett.

"There’s no benefit in rushing to sow grass seed if it’s not going to have the right conditions to germinate and establish well.”

So if temperatures haven’t yet dropped, what is the best method for overseeding a lawn? To give your lawn an optimal head start in establishing healthy grass, experts suggest sowing a fast-germinating seed mix.

“If the conditions are mild enough, choose a fast-germinating grass seed mix such as one containing perennial ryegrass,” adds Bonnett. “This will help give your lawn the best chance of establishing.”

Of course, preparation is essential, so start by eliminating weeds, clearing leaves, and leveling the ground with a rake before you start seeding.

“Scatter the seed evenly and gently rake it into the top layer of the soil. Keep the area slightly moist but avoid overwatering, especially in November when rainfall is more frequent. If the ground is already wet or waterlogged, avoid planting.”

For more top tips, check out how to overseed your lawn in fall for the best results in spring.
